clue.text: Deadlock involving British chum at one's club?

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so the word for deadlock wraps around the letter for British

parts.note: a deadlock with no way forward is a stalemate, as in chess

explanation.surface: A stalemate somehow involves a British friend at a gentlemen's club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' puts B inside STALEMATE. The question mark flags the definition: a stablemate is properly a horse from the same stable, so a fellow club member is a playful extension.
explanation.definitionFit: A stablemate is a companion from the same organisation or group, such as a fellow member of a club.

clue.text: You aren't half grand!

indicators.note: aren't half signals that only the front half of the word for grand is wanted

parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: An exclamation that the listener is truly magnificent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aren't half' is the British idiom for 'really are', which hides the instruction: take half of THOUSAND (from 'grand'), its first four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Thou is the old second-person singular pronoun, the archaic form of address.

clue.text: Busy person, given something to eat, grumbled

parts.note: a busy person is a bee, from the phrase 'busy as a bee'
someone given something to eat has been fed

explanation.surface: A hard-working person complained after being fed.
explanation.definitionFit: To beef is slang for to complain, so beefed is a past-tense synonym of grumbled.

clue.text: Bias shown with president lacking charm

indicators.note: lacking means without, so the letter for president drops out of the word for bias

parts.note: a bias or leaning towards something is a penchant

explanation.surface: A president's prejudice is revealed and he has no charisma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' removes P from PENCHANT. 'charm' looks like a noun after 'lacking', but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To enchant is to delight or bewitch, a verb synonym of charm.

clue.text: River in which star is reflected

indicators.note: a mirror image runs the other way, so the word for star is read backwards

parts.note: a nova is a star that suddenly brightens

explanation.surface: A river whose surface mirrors a star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is reflected' turns NOVA round. The Avon flows through Stratford, Shakespeare's town.
explanation.definitionFit: The Avon is one of several English rivers of that name, notably the one at Stratford.

clue.text: Oriental knight appears at end of festival

indicators.note: the letter for knight comes after the festival word, at its end

parts.note: Easter is the Christian spring festival
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: An Eastern knight turns up as a festival closes.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriental and eastern both describe things from the East, so they are adjectival synonyms.

clue.text: What the elderly suffer from in our era

explanation.surface: A remark on old age in the present day.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'in the year of our Lord', it marks the Christian era, and is joking slang for advancing age.

clue.text: Such are church weddings, one's smiled stupidly

indicators.note: doing something stupidly suggests disorder, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: At a church wedding, one has grinned foolishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stupidly' rearranges ONES and SMILED into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A marriage performed with religious ceremony is formally solemnised.

clue.text: Enthusiastic about some paint — oils, I think

indicators.note: some of the words means only a stretch of their letters is taken

explanation.surface: Someone thinks they are keen on paint, oils in particular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' points to the letters running across 'paINT Oils'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being into something is informal for being keen on it.

clue.text: Don't go down for encounter

explanation.surface: An instruction against descent, offered as a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: In a crossword, lights go across or down, so 'Don't go down' is read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: To meet by chance is to come across someone; in grid terms, not going down means travelling horizontally.

clue.text: Monarchy discountenanced from what we hear

indicators.note: from what we hear says the word is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: someone discountenanced is disconcerted, or thrown

explanation.surface: Monarchy is reported to have been put out of countenance.
explanation.definitionFit: The throne stands for royal power, so it can mean the monarchy itself.

clue.text: Arrival of Scottish author, big noise coming in

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so the word for noise goes inside the author's name

parts.note: Andrew Lang was a Scottish writer known for his fairy books
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A Scottish writer arrives amid a loud racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming in' is the container signal. Andrew Lang is fair game as a 'Scottish author' because crosswords lean on him for his short surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A landing is the arrival of an aircraft or boat at the ground or shore.

clue.text: Elder son — he ruined trousers

indicators.note: ruined suggests the words are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: An older son has spoiled a pair of trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges ELDERSONHE. Lederhosen are Bavarian leather shorts.
explanation.definitionFit: Lederhosen are leather shorts with braces, a kind of Alpine legwear.

clue.text: Unpleasant experiences near turbulent stream

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Unpleasant experiences near turbulent stream (10)': NEAR STREAM cannot be rearranged into NIGHTMARES, and no other reading builds it; the clue seems garbled or cut short, and a search found no other version

clue.text: Filling in the cracks is little good — heavy defeat ensues

parts.note: G is a short form of good
a rout is a crushing defeat

explanation.surface: A minor success is followed by a hammering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ensues' just keeps the order: ROUT comes after G.
explanation.definitionFit: Grout is mortar used to fill the gaps between tiles.

clue.text: Hat almost ridiculous, ripped on the outside

indicators.note: on the outside means the word for ripped encloses the rest

parts.note: ripped means torn

indicators.note: almost means one letter short, so the final letter of the word for ridiculous goes

parts.note: rich in the sense of absurd, as in 'that's rich'

explanation.surface: A hat that looks a bit silly and is torn on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims the last letter of the synonym, and 'on the outside' makes the word for ripped the container. 'ridiculous' meaning rich is the British 'that's rich!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tricorn is a three-cornered hat of the eighteenth century.

clue.text: The little boy I had is shy

parts.note: Tim is a boy's name, a short form of Timothy
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: A parent says their small son is bashful.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiny Tim of Dickens's A Christmas Carol may lie behind 'The little boy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Timid and shy both describe someone lacking confidence.

clue.text: Coach artist wanting to get in the money

indicators.note: to get in means entering, so the artist's letters go inside the word for money

parts.note: tin is old British slang for money
RA is a Royal Academician, a recognised artist

explanation.surface: An artist hoping to break into the cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get in' is the container signal. 'Coach' looks like a vehicle, but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To coach someone is to train them, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Venetian bigwig? Someone not nice to English

parts.note: dog is a contemptuous term for a nasty person

explanation.surface: A Venetian grandee who is unpleasant to the English.
explanation.definitionFit: The doge was the elected chief magistrate of Venice.

clue.text: Hello, saints may be making an unwelcome noise!

parts.note: hi is an informal hello
S is short for saint, so SS is saints

explanation.surface: Greeting saints might draw a sound of disapproval.
explanation.definitionFit: A hiss is the sibilant sound an audience makes in disapproval.

clue.text: Young whelp, one learner — is that what he is?

definitions.text: Young whelp, one learner — is that what he is?

parts.note: a whelp is a young dog, a pup
I is the Roman numeral one
L is for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: Asking whether a young cub of a student is really a learner.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: a young learner is exactly a schoolchild.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolchild being taught is a student, which is what a young learner is.

clue.text: Lords always needing attendant around

indicators.note: around means the attendant's word surrounds the word for always

parts.note: a page is a young attendant
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, always

explanation.surface: Peers always need an attendant at their side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' is the container signal; 'needing' only links. 'Lords' is the house of peers taken collectively.
explanation.definitionFit: The peerage is the body of peers, the lords of the realm collectively.

clue.text: Trees replanted by Charles

indicators.note: replanted means put in again in a new arrangement, a hint to rearrange the name

explanation.surface: Charles has replanted some trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replanted' rearranges CHARLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Larches are deciduous conifers, a kind of tree.

clue.text: Part of machine making awful chatter

indicators.note: awful signals the letters are dreadfully jumbled

explanation.surface: A machine part making a horrible chattering noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges CHATTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratchet is a toothed mechanism allowing motion in one direction only.

clue.text: Daughter in union — but took time!

parts.note: nations in union are allied

explanation.surface: A daughter got married, but only after taking her time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in union' reads like a wedding, but it is ALLIED; 'in' is not a container signal here.
explanation.definitionFit: To dally is to dawdle or linger, so dallied means lingered.

clue.text: Cast-off stuff giving lake a brown colour

parts.note: L is the map abbreviation for lake
umber is a brown earth pigment

explanation.surface: Discarded things turn a lake brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumber is British for unwanted junk stored away, such as old furniture.

clue.text: King's daughter coming round on old ass

indicators.note: coming round means turning back, so the pieces are read in reverse

parts.note: Regan is one of King Lear's daughters in Shakespeare

explanation.surface: A princess returns riding an aged donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming round' turns REGAN plus O backwards. 'King's daughter' is Lear's, not any royal's.
explanation.definitionFit: An onager is a wild ass of Asia.

clue.text: A very old railway gets gifts

parts.note: LMS was the London, Midland and Scottish Railway, merged into British Railways in 1948

explanation.surface: An old railway company receives donations.
explanation.definitionFit: Alms are charitable donations given to the poor.

clue.text: Man, maybe — and what Donne implied he wasn't

explanation.surface: A reflection on John Donne's view of man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea; Donne wrote 'No man is an island'.
explanation.definitionFit: An island is a small land mass: Man is one example, and Donne's line denies any person is one.

clue.text: Nothing inferior in greeting

explanation.surface: A greeting that promises only top quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Having only the finest items is having nothing second-rate; the phrase is also a parting good wish.

clue.text: Calm time when sun goes down for the poet

definitions.text: time when sun goes down for the poet

explanation.surface: A peaceful moment at dusk, in verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Even means level or placid; poets use the same word for evening.

clue.text: The way of the idle rich?

definitions.text: The way of the idle rich?

parts.words: The way of the idle rich?
parts.note: a road name standing for a comfortable life without work or money worries

explanation.surface: A question about how wealthy people who never work live.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on this street is an idiom for living in comfort and affluence.
